About

Syahzani

The short version

I am a product designer working on operational software: enterprise platforms, support desks, and the tablet mounted behind a bar. The kind of product people sit inside for eight hours, until they know where every button lives.

I usually get called in once a product has grown one feature at a time and nobody can describe it in a sentence any more. My job is to give it back a shape someone can defend in a review.

Get the model honest, and the interface becomes the easy part.

How I work

Sit with it firstInterviews and shadowing before anything gets drawn. I write down every place people route around the software.
Model itObjects, states and permissions agreed before the first screen. It is faster to argue about a diagram than a prototype.
Ship the systemTokens, components and written hand-off, so the twentieth screen still looks like the first without me in the room.

What I go deep on

The part that rarely shows up in a portfolio shot: how an object is modelled, who is allowed to change what, and whether a decision still makes sense six months later when nobody remembers the reasoning. Permission models, state machines and information architecture are where I do my most useful work.

I stay through build. I sit in the sprint, answer the edge cases, and cut scope with the engineers when the date is real. Design that ships is the only kind that counts.

Before this

Earlier work was consumer apps and marketing sites, and that experience still earns its keep: writing interfaces that make sense to someone opening them for the very first time.

Outside work

Coffee brewed with more equipment than any morning deserves, and a font collection I keep adding to and rarely use.

UI/UX Case Study

Eleven departments.
One company.
One coherent system.

by Syahzani Enterprise operations platform · Research, IA, system, UI
vnt.networks/hc/dashboard
Role
Product Designer · UX
Surface
Enterprise web platform
Scope
Research · IA · System · UI
Year
2026

Overview

VNT Networks runs an internet-service business, from people and sales through to delivery and finance, on a single operating platform.

The mandate wasn’t to draw screens. It was to make a sprawling organisation feel like one product, where every role sees the slice they need and nothing they don’t. An ISP is not one business; it is a dozen interlocking ones, and each arrived with its own vocabulary, its own tools, and its own idea of what “a customer” even is.

Context

Each function on its own tool
Work crossed teams; the software didn’t. Hand-offs lived in spreadsheets, chat and memory.

Mandate

Unify without flattening
One platform, without collapsing eleven very different jobs into one generic screen.

Approach

A shared spine, then surfaces
Design the spine first: navigation, identity, workspace. Then let each department compose on top of it.

Outcome

Scales by addition
New departments slot into the same spine; people move between them without relearning.

A note on the screens that follow. They are captured from a super-admin account, which is why one profile can open Human Capital, Sales and the shared Workspace in the same session. That account exists for platform owners and support. Everyone else signs in to the same spine and sees only the surfaces their job needs: a recruiter never lands in the payroll ledger, and a sales rep never sees the org chart. Role-scoped access is the point of the design, and the super-admin view is simply the one vantage point that can show all of it in a single case study.

What’s in this case study

Nine sections · roughly twelve minutes · jump anywhere

01The complexity, honestlyEleven departments, dozens of modules, hundreds of states 02How I reasoned about itSix laws that each settled a specific argument 03The operating principleA spine in the middle, departments on top, a shared desk underneath 04Where this sits in the landscapeHonest about what SAP, NetSuite, Odoo and Salesforce each trade away 05Department I: Human CapitalOne employee, one lifecycle, from job posting to payslip 06Department II: SalesLead to revenue as one line a rep can walk 07The shared WorkspaceCalendar, tasks, mail and files as a first-class layer 08What it changesBaselines, design targets, and what I would measure 09ReflectionFewer ideas, applied consistently

The complexity, honestly

Before clarity, you have to look the mess in the eye

SECTION 01

The mess,
mapped

Sales closes a contract; delivery provisions it; operations keeps it alive; finance bills it; people staff all of it. Each function arrived with its own vocabulary, its own tools, and its own idea of what a customer is.

Mapping it produced a daunting picture: eleven departments, dozens of modules, hundreds of states, and a single employee who might touch five of them before lunch. The naive fix is to ship eleven apps. The trap is that the work doesn’t respect those walls; it flows across them all day.

VNT · one spine
Human Capital
Sales
Workspace

Project

Fig. 01 · the platform surface area, mapped. Solid tiles are the three areas deep-dived in this study.
SECTION 02

How I reasoned about it

Big systems reward people who design from principle, not from screens.

Each law below resolved a specific argument about where complexity should live and what should stay constant. The most useful frame was Conway’s Law: software tends to mirror the organisation that builds and uses it. Rather than fight that, I made it intentional, departments as clean bounded contexts on a shared spine, not accidental silos.

Conway’s Law

Systems mirror the organisations that use them.
Departments are deliberate bounded contexts on one spine, mirrored on purpose, not fragmented by accident.

Tesler’s Law

Complexity is conserved, it can be moved but not erased.
The platform absorbs the irreducible complexity so the operator doesn’t. Defaults, states and rules live in the system.

Jakob’s Law

People expect your product to work like the others they know.
The spine reuses familiar enterprise patterns, so moving between departments feels like the same product.

Hick’s Law

More choices, slower decisions.
Role-scoped surfaces show a person only the modules their job needs, fewer options and faster action.

Single source of truth

One canonical record, referenced everywhere.
One customer object, one employee object. Other modules reference, never re-key, so data can’t diverge.

Progressive disclosure

Surface the essential; reveal depth on demand.
Dashboards open on the one number a role cares about; the long tail of detail is a click away.

Underneath, every surface was specified with a Jobs-to-be-Done lens, designed around the outcome a role is hiring the software for, not the features it happens to contain.

SECTION 03

The operating principle

A spine in the middle. Departments on top. A shared desk underneath.

Those laws converge on one structure: a three-layer system. It is the single idea the whole platform rests on, and it is why the product can grow without collapsing under its own weight.

Layer 1

The spine
One navigation, one identity, one design language. You always know where you are and what the controls mean. Jakob’s Law, made literal.

Layer 2

Department surfaces
Each function composes its own modules and language on top of the spine, as a bounded context. Conway’s Law, channelled.

Layer 3

The Workspace
Calendar, tasks, mail and files that every department shares, so cross-team work never leaves the platform.
Consistency where it builds trust; difference where the job demands it. That balance is the entire design.
vnt.networks/sales/dashboard
One spine, alwaysNavigation, identity and the design language stay put as you move between departments.
Surfaces differ on purposeSales composes its own modules on top of that spine, deliberate difference rather than accidental drift.
Sales, composed on the same spine as Human Capital. The chrome is identical, only the surface changes. Both are shot from the super-admin account, the one role that can open every department.

Where this sits in the landscape

The giants are powerful. They are also someone else’s shape.

SECTION 04

Benchmark

I benchmarked the approach against the tools a mid-market ISP would actually evaluate. The point isn’t to “beat SAP”, it is to be honest about the trade each one makes, and to locate VNT’s distinct bet: a shared spine plus a native workspace layer, the two things the heavyweights tend to treat as configuration or add-ons.

CapabilityVNTSAP S/4HANAOracle NetSuiteOdooSalesforcemonday.com
One unified spine · single IA & login●◐ modular●◐◐ CRM-led● light
Role-scoped surfaces (per job, not per feature)●◐ config-heavy◐◐●◐
Native shared workspace (mail · tasks · files)●— add-on◐◐ apps◐● PM-only
One customer & employee record across departments●●●◐◐ HR add-on—
Low relearning when switching departments●— steep◐◐◐●
Extends by addition on the same spine●◐ heavy●● modular◐ apps● light
Fit for SEA ISP mid-market● tailored— enterprise◐● SMB◐ CRM◐ generic

● strong · ◐ partial or with effort · — weak or via add-ons. Read it this way: SAP and NetSuite win on depth but tax the user with complexity and a steep curve; Odoo is modular yet fragmented across apps; Salesforce owns the CRM motion but isn’t whole-company ops; monday is friendly but not ERP-grade. VNT’s wedge is the spine plus a native workspace, operational breadth that still feels like one learnable product.

Department I: Human Capital

One employee, one lifecycle, from a job posting to a payslip, without leaving the spine

SECTION 05

One lifecycle,
not four inboxes

People work spans four sub-functions that rarely talk: talent acquisition, people operations, the HR generalist desk, and general affairs. I modelled them as stages of one lifecycle rather than separate inboxes, a candidate becomes a pre-employee, then an employee with attendance, leave, payroll and growth, all carrying the same identity forward.

The win is continuity. The data a recruiter captures at application is the same record payroll trusts months later. No re-entry, no divergence, one source of truth for a human being. That single decision quietly removes a whole category of HR errors.

Recruiter
“When a role opens, help me move candidates to a decision fast, and hand the winner off without re-typing them.”
People Ops
“When the month closes, let me run attendance, leave and payroll from records I already trust.”
HR lead
“When I open the platform, show me headcount and people-health for a decision, not a data dump.”
vnt.networks/hc/dashboard
vnt.networks/people-ops/payroll
The org at a glanceHeadcount, pipeline and people-health framed for a decision, progressive disclosure rather than a data dump.
Same person, later stagePayroll reads the identity captured at hiring. One record, no re-entry, no divergence.
Human Capital dashboard, then Payroll, two stages of one employee lifecycle. The profile in the corner stays the same because this is the super-admin view; a recruiter would only ever reach the first of these two screens.

Department II: Sales

Turn a scattered pipeline into a single line a rep can walk: lead to revenue

SECTION 06

The customer
is one object

Sales lived across spreadsheets, inboxes and memory. The redesign threads the whole motion into one continuous surface, lead → opportunity → quotation → RFC → project, with a dashboard that answers “where’s my number?” the moment a rep logs in.

Crucially, a closed deal doesn’t dead-end in Sales. It becomes a delivery project on the same spine, so the customer is one object the whole company can see, the same record delivery, finance and ops all reference. Sell-side and deliver-side stop arguing about whose spreadsheet is right.

vnt.networks/sales/my-customer
One number, firstThe dashboard opens on target versus achievement, the question every rep actually has.
The customer is one objectContracts, services, health and renewals on a single record, shared across departments.
The account record that survives the hand-off from Sales into delivery.
SECTION 07

The shared Workspace

The connective tissue every department stands on.

Cross-team work is where most enterprise tools leak into email and chat. So calendar, tasks, mail, files and policy aren’t bolted on, they are a first-class layer beneath every department. An HR officer assigns onboarding tasks, a sales rep schedules a site survey, and both live in the same Workspace, governed by the same spine.

It’s the quiet decision that keeps the platform whole: collaboration never has to leave the building.

vnt.networks/workspace/calendar
A layer, not an add-onCalendar, tasks, mail, files and policy sit beneath every department rather than beside them.
Same spine, same rulesAn HR officer assigning onboarding and a rep booking a site survey work in one place, governed identically.
The shared Workspace with Calendar open. Tasks, mail, cloud and policy live on that same layer.

SECTION 09

Reflection

Enterprise UX isn’t about more screens. It’s about fewer ideas, applied consistently.

The hard part of a platform this wide isn’t any single screen, it is deciding what stays the same everywhere so that what differs can differ safely. Conway’s Law says the system will mirror the organisation regardless; the craft is making that mirror deliberate.

Get the spine right and the product compounds: every new department makes the next one cheaper to design and easier to learn. That’s the lens I bring to scale, treat the system as the product, ground each decision in a principle I can defend, and the interface becomes the easy part.

Designed so the whole company feels like one product.

UI/UX Case Study

Support isn’t a queue.
It’s an organisation.

by Syahzani Omnichannel support platform · Research, IA, interaction, system
helix.app/inbox
Role
Product Designer · UX
Surface
Web app · operations tool
Scope
Research · IA · Interaction · System
Year
2026

Overview

Most support tools hand every agent the same screen and hope for the best.

Helix is a redesign that treats a support team as what it really is, people with different roles, authority and accountability, and builds the interface around that single stubborn truth. The brief looked like “redesign an inbox”. The actual problem was coordination under pressure.

Context

A busy floor at peak
Conversations arrive from WhatsApp, email and web at once, and two agents can open the same thread.

The real cost

Ambiguity, not volume
When an SLA breaches, no tool could answer: who owned this, and when did it change hands?

Approach

Design the rules first
Model perspective, accountability and authority, then let the interface compose itself from them.

Outcome

One product, many truths
The same screen reads differently per role, with ownership and permission legible at all times.

What’s in this case study

Seven sections · roughly nine minutes · jump anywhere

01The premiseBy 4 p.m. the queue has won, and nobody can say who dropped the ball 02The reframeThree flat features became three first-class concepts 03One app, many truths“View as”, the same screen read three ways 04Accountability is an objectA state machine, an audit trail, and first-click-wins locking 05Authority you can reason aboutPermissions as one legible matrix, not patches in the UI 06The room, at a glanceWorkload, SLA health and a live queue, every number a doorway 07Trade-offs & reflectionWhat I chose, what I gave up, and what I would do next

The premise

By 4 p.m. the queue has won. And nobody can say who dropped the ball.

SECTION 01

Coordination under pressure

An agent is mid-reply when a teammate, three desks over, opens the same conversation. Neither of them knows.
Observed on a support floor at peak, across WhatsApp, email and web arriving at once.
A supervisor needs to rebalance a colleague quietly drowning under eighteen open threads, but the tools show her the same flat list everyone else sees.
The lead has authority to act, and no surface that makes the problem visible in time.
When an SLA breaches, the post-mortem asks the one question no tool could answer: who owned this, and when did it change hands?
That ambiguity, not message volume, is the real cost. It erodes trust inside the team and with the customer.
SECTION 02

The reframe

So I stopped designing a list, and started designing a system of roles.

Interviews with agents, leads and operations managers kept returning the same shape: the friction wasn’t reading messages, it was knowing your place in the machine: what you are responsible for, what you are allowed to do, and what is happening to the work around you.

That reframed three flat features into three first-class concepts the whole product is organised around. Everything downstream, the inbox, the dashboard and the permissions, is just these three ideas made visible.

Perspective

The same data should read differently depending on who you are.
“View as” became a built-in control, not a debugging trick.

Accountability

Ownership is an object with a history, not a vibe.
Every transition writes an immutable line in an audit timeline.

Authority

What you can do should be legible, never a surprise.
One permission matrix drives every gated action in the product.
SECTION 03

One app, many truths

The same screen should tell a different story to each person reading it.

A frontline agent and an operations lead do not need the same inbox, but they should live in the same product, so context is never lost in a hand-off. So I made perspective a built-in control: “View as” lets you step into any role, or even a customer’s shoes, and the data, permissions and emphasis re-compose around them.

It started as a debugging affordance for me. It became one of the most loved features, useful for onboarding, QA and empathy, all from one switch.

helix.app/inbox
AgentSees the threads they own and the actions policy allows, nothing they must ask permission for.
SupervisorSame conversation, but ownership, SLA risk and reassignment surface first, because that is the job.
One screen, read two ways. “View as” re-composes the data, permissions and emphasis around the role.

Accountability is an object

Two agents reach for the same conversation. Only one can win, and the record must say so.

SECTION 04

Ownership,
with a history

If ownership is fuzzy, work is either dropped or done twice. So I treated it as a real object with a state machine, unassigned → owned → reassigned → resolved, and gave every transition an immutable line in an audit timeline. No silent hand-offs.

The sharp edge is concurrency. When two people click the same thread at once, the interface resolves it with atomic, first-click-wins assignment: the winner gets it, the loser is told instantly and gracefully, not with a stale screen and a collision an hour later.

Conversation #C8 · state: unassigned
Sarah clicks · t+0 ms
Marco clicks · t+9 ms
LOCK acquired · first write wins
Sarah → owner · audit logged
Marco → “claimed by Sarah”
Fig. 01 · assignment as a decision, resolved atomically rather than optimistically.
SECTION 05

Authority you can reason about

A permission model is a UX problem before it’s a security one.

If people can’t predict what they are allowed to do, they hesitate, escalate needlessly, or work around the system. So permissions live in a single legible matrix, roles down one axis and capabilities across the other, and the same rules drive what every button does. The interface never offers an action it will later refuse.

CapabilityAgentSeniorSupervisorAdmin
Reply & resolve (in policy)✓✓✓✓
Request reassignmentlead approval✓✓✓
Reassign / approve——✓✓
Override lock——with reason✓
Dashboards & SLA—team✓✓
Settings & automation———✓

Fig. 02 · capability × role, an excerpt of the live matrix. It is the actual decision surface in the product, not a diagram of one: editing a cell here changes what the interface offers.

helix.app/settings/roles
The live decision surfaceThis grid is not a diagram of the model, editing a cell changes what the interface offers.
Legible by designRoles down one axis, capabilities across the other, so nobody has to guess what they may do.
The Roles & Permissions surface in the product, seen from the admin POV.
SECTION 06

The room,
at a glance

A lead should feel the floor’s health in one breath, then act in one click.

The operations view answers three questions fast: where is load piling up, what is at SLA risk, and what is happening right now. Workload distribution, SLA health and a live queue sit on one surface, and every number is a doorway: click a spike to open exactly the conversations behind it.

It closes the loop with everything before it. Spot an overloaded teammate here, and the reassignment you trigger is governed by the same permissions and written to the same audit trail.

helix.app/dashboard
Every number is a doorwayClick a spike in the workload distribution and the exact conversations behind it open.
One breath, then one clickLoad, SLA health and the live queue on one surface, and any reassignment obeys the same permissions.
Operations Overview, where a lead feels the floor’s health and then acts on it.

What I chose, and what I gave up

Maturity in design is owning the cost of a decision

SECTION 07

Trade-offs

Chose

First-click-wins locking. Predictable and honest under contention.

Gave up

A small share of “I clicked first!” disputes, softened with an instant and kind rejection state.

Chose

One product, many points of view. Shared context, zero hand-off loss.

Gave up

A leaner build. Re-composing per role is real engineering and design cost.

Chose

Permissions as one visible matrix. Legible, auditable, predictable.

Gave up

Maximum flexibility, deliberately fewer bespoke per-user exceptions.

Reflection

I don’t design screens. I design the rules that make a hundred screens behave.

Helix taught me that the highest-leverage UX work often hides below the surface, in how state, ownership and authority are modelled. Get the system honest, and the interface almost designs itself: the agent trusts the tool, the lead trusts the floor, and the customer feels the difference without knowing why.

If I carried it forward, I would push the same idea into prediction, surfacing the overload before 4 p.m. and proposing the rebalance instead of waiting to be asked.

Designed to be reasoned about, not just used.

UI/UX Case Study

Music, properly licensed.
Scheduled by the hour.
Built for the floor.

by Syahzani Commercial music platform · UX, UI, design system
Role
Product Designer, end to end
Platform
Tablet-first web app
Scope
UX · UI · Design System
Year
2026

Overview

Velodiva is the music system a business actually runs on, not the playlist someone forgot to pause.

Most venues still play music the wrong way: a personal streaming account behind the counter, no licence for commercial use, and a vibe that drifts the moment the morning barista leaves. It is legally exposed, operationally fragile, and disconnected from how the business performs.

Velodiva replaces all of that with one commercial music platform built for the people who run the room. Every track is cleared for venue playback with royalties included. Playlists are time-blocked by service period, so the room sounds right from open to close without anyone touching it. And for the first time, what is playing is connected to what is selling.

It ships as a tablet-first app that lives on the counter, readable across a busy floor, locked down for staff, and fluent in six languages for teams across Southeast Asia.

What’s in this case study

Six sections · roughly ten minutes · jump anywhere

01The challengeFour tensions: licensing risk, drift, many hands, no feedback loop 02Research & discovery27 venue types, and the one truth they shared 03A design language for the floorRead across a noisy room, not six inches from your face 04Five surfaces that matterEach one removes a specific anxiety from the operator’s day 05ImpactWhat the design set out to change, and how it would be measured 06ReflectionMaking compliance feel like care

The challenge

Consumer-grade experience, enterprise-grade compliance, thirty seconds between customers

SECTION 01

Four tensions shaped every decision

Licensing risk

Commercial playback needs PRO coverage and auditable royalty reporting.
Invisible to most operators until a fine arrives, so it had to become visible and calm.

The room drifts

Energy needs to change across the day.
Nobody has time to re-curate between the morning rush and dinner, so the schedule must run itself.

Many hands

Owners, managers and rotating floor staff touch the same device.
Very different needs and trust levels, so two postures on one tablet.

No feedback loop

Music was a cost and a guess.
Never tied back to dwell time, footfall or sales, until the POS connection closed the loop.
Make commercial music feel as effortless as Spotify, as trustworthy as an accountant, and as operable as a light switch.
SECTION 02

Research & discovery

We mapped 27 venue types, and found one truth they shared.

From specialty coffee to hotel lobbies, gyms and retail, the work served wildly different rooms. On-site observation across these contexts surfaced a shared pattern: the person controlling the music is rarely the person who chose it, and almost never the person worried about the licence.

That insight split the product into two postures: a rich management view for owners (scheduling, licensing, insights) and a locked, simplified view for floor staff. It also pushed localisation to the front: real teams here work in Indonesian, Malay, Vietnamese, Thai, Chinese and English, often within the same chain.

27
venue industries supported, from cafés to fitness
6
languages, built in from day one for SEA teams
2
operating postures: manager, and PIN-locked staff
100%
of catalogue cleared for commercial playback
SECTION 03

A design language for the floor

Dark, glassy and high-contrast, engineered to be read across a noisy room rather than held six inches from your face.

The interface runs on a deep near-black canvas with layered glass surfaces, so album art and the brand’s warm gradient do the talking. A single magenta-to-amber gradient marks identity and primary action, while a disciplined semantic palette carries meaning the operator can trust at a glance.

Brand gradientIdentity · primary action
ComplianceLicensed · royalties on
WarningFees & renewals
CriticalOffline · action needed
DiscoverSuggestions & AI
HeritageCurated & editorial

Type scale

Tight and structural, an eleven-step scale from a 36px display down to 10px eyebrows, paired with generous radii and a snappy, physical motion curve so the tablet feels alive but never fussy.

36 / 800Display
22 / 800Heading One
17 / 700Section title
13 / 400Body, calm and dense, scannable across the floor.
  • 76 → 232px sidebar that expands on intent
  • 320px right panel, the persistent now-playing rail
  • Glass cards with inset highlights and soft depth
  • Light and dark themes from one token set

Five surfaces that matter

Velodiva is broad, but five experiences carry the product’s promise

SECTION 04

Each one removes an anxiety

FEATURE 01 · COMPLIANCE

The License Vault

Licensing was the scariest, most invisible part of running music in a venue, so I made it the calmest screen in the app. The Vault gathers every PRO, certificate and royalty estimate into one place, with coverage stated plainly and renewals surfaced before they bite.

  • All-rights coverage shown as a single confidence number
  • Monthly royalty estimates in local currency (IDR 248k · 47h playback)
  • Downloadable certificates, audit-ready, per venue
  • Proactive alerts: “commercial fees rise 5% Jul 2026”
Coverage, not jargonOne confidence number answers the only question an owner has: am I covered right now?
Audit-readyA verifiable certificate, a royalty estimate in local currency, and renewals surfaced before they bite.
The License Vault, the riskiest part of the job, designed as the calmest screen in the app.
FEATURE 02 · OPERATIONS

Time-blocked scheduling

A café isn’t one mood, it’s a morning, a lull, a rush and a wind-down. The scheduler lets an owner block the day into service periods, each with its own playlist, then walk away. Music auto-switches by operating hours; staff never have to curate live.

  • Up to six blocks spanning 07:00–24:00, per template
  • Auto-switch by operating hours, with a 24/7 option
  • Schedule Health flags gaps and abrupt energy jumps
  • Day templates, a different shape for Saturday
Set it, then walk awayEach block carries its own playlist; the day switches itself so nobody curates during service.
Schedule HealthGaps and abrupt energy jumps are flagged before the room ever hears them.
Time-blocked scheduling, up to six service periods, auto-switching by operating hours.
FEATURE 03 · INTELLIGENCE

POS Insights

The feature that turns music from a cost into a lever. By connecting the venue’s point-of-sale, Velodiva correlates what is playing with how people behave, then frames it as gentle, human guidance rather than opaque scores.

  • Music-to-behaviour signals: “guests dwell 18% longer 4–6 PM”
  • Plain-language insights and recommendations, not dashboards
  • Suggested mixes that respect operating hours
  • An engagement digest owners actually read
Guidance, not scoresA sentence an owner can act on beats a chart they have to interpret mid-shift.
The loop finally closesConnecting the point-of-sale turns music from a cost and a guess into something measurable.
POS Insights, what is playing set against how people actually behave.
FEATURE 04 · ENGAGEMENT

Guest song requests

Guests can shape the room without an app or an account. A table QR opens a request flow; staff see an approval queue that respects the brand and the schedule, so the floor stays on-vibe while customers feel heard.

  • No app needed, scan, search and request from any phone
  • Staff approval queue with one-tap accept and “approve all”
  • Requests blend into rotation without breaking the mood
  • Master switch to enable per venue or per shift
Heard, but on-brandRequests pass a staff approval queue, so the floor stays on-vibe while guests feel listened to.
No app, no accountA table QR opens the request flow on any phone.
Guest requests, participation without handing the room over.
FEATURE 05 · TRUST AND CONTROL

Remote, Staff Mode and six languages

The last mile is about who can do what, from where, in which language. Remote control runs off a QR, adjust playback from any phone, no install. Staff Mode strips the UI to essentials behind a PIN, so a new hire can’t break the schedule or expose billing. And every surface speaks the team’s language.

  • Remote control via QR from any phone
  • Staff Mode, simplified UI with PIN-locked navigation
  • Zones and multi-device: indoor, patio, restroom
  • Localised for ID, MS, VI, TH, ZH and EN
Two postures, one deviceThe owner gets scheduling, licensing and insights. Behind a PIN, staff get play, pause and volume.
Six languagesID, MS, VI, TH, ZH and EN, because a chain’s teams rarely share one language.
Remote control over QR, plus the PIN-locked Staff Mode that keeps the schedule safe.

Impact

What the design set out to change, stated plainly and with its status

SECTION 05

What it changes

100%
licensed playback, commercial risk designed out
~0
daily curation once the day is scheduled
+18%
guest dwell during optimised afternoon blocks
6
languages live, ready for regional rollout

Figures shown are illustrative for this case-study narrative, drawn from the product’s own scenarios and data points. Swap them for verified results before publishing.

SECTION 06

Reflection

The hardest part wasn’t the music, it was making compliance feel like care.

When the riskiest screen becomes the calmest one, you know the system is finally working for the person behind the counter.

Velodiva taught me to design for two users on one device, the owner who wants control and the staffer who wants to not break anything, and to treat legal trust as a first-class experience rather than fine print. Next, I would push the POS loop further: from describing what happened to gently proposing what to play next.

Designing systems that make the everyday business feel effortless.

UI/UX Case Study

A packaging factory,
rebuilt as a shop window

by Syahzani Marketing website · Research, IA, UI, design system, responsive
flexypack.co.id
Role
Product Designer · UI
Surface
Responsive marketing site
Scope
IA · UI · Design system
Year
2026

Overview

FlexyPack prints flexible packaging for beauty brands. The website had to sell a factory to people who have never briefed one.

The customer here is usually a founder with a good formula, a small budget and no packaging vocabulary. They do not know what a standing pouch costs, what a minimum order quantity means for their cash, or why one material protects a serum better than another. A brochure site would list capabilities at them. This one had to teach, reassure and quote, in that order.

So the page is built as a funnel rather than a catalogue: recognise your own product first, understand why this supplier is safe, see proof it has been done before, then ask for a price. Everything on the page earns its place by moving someone one step further along that line.

Context

A factory, not a brand
Strong printing capability, no shop window. Enquiries arrived through chat with no shared language for materials or sizes.

Audience

First-time founders
Skincare, cosmetics and wellness brands ordering packaging for the first time, often in small runs.

Approach

Teach, then quote
Category first, material second, technology third, price last. Each section answers the question the previous one raises.

Deliverable

Site plus system
A responsive marketing site and a written design style profile: colour, type, spacing, components, motion, voice, accessibility.

What’s in this case study

Six sections · roughly nine minutes · jump anywhere

01The page as a funnelFourteen blocks, each answering the question before it 02Teaching without a lectureMaterials and print technology explained in the buyer’s words 03The visual systemOne typeface, a disciplined palette, a 4px rhythm 04Responsive by rule, not by eyeThree breakpoints, and a table that decides every padding 05Earning the enquiryProof, process and the questions people actually ask 06ReflectionWhat a style profile buys you after hand-off

The page as a funnel

Fourteen blocks, ordered so each one answers the question the previous one raises

SECTION 01

Start where
the buyer starts

A founder does not arrive wanting “flexible packaging”. They arrive wanting a pouch for their serum. So the first thing under the hero is not a company profile, it is a row of product categories in the buyer’s own words: serum, standing pouch, sachet, body lotion, hair care. Recognition before education.

Only once someone has found their own product does the page start explaining. Six reasons to choose this supplier, then a gallery of work already printed, then materials, then the press itself. The order is deliberate: every block answers a doubt raised by the one above it, and the price conversation waits until the doubts are gone.

flexypack.co.id
Their words, not oursCategories are named after what the founder is making, so nobody has to translate a product into a packaging format.
Objections, coloured inMOQ, design freedom, print quality, food grade, speed and expert help, each given its own solid card.
The two blocks that follow the hero: find yourself, then find a reason to stay.
PROOF

Show the work before claiming the skill

The gallery sits above the technical sections on purpose. Filters by category let someone check that their kind of product has been printed here before, which is a faster form of trust than any paragraph about capability.

flexypack.co.id/#inspirasi
Inspiration gallery. Filter chips carry the same category names used higher up the page.

Teaching without a lecture

Materials and print technology, explained the way a buyer would ask about them

SECTION 02

Five materials,
one sentence each

Material choice is where first-time buyers freeze. Each of the five options gets a photograph, one plain sentence about what it is good at, and the product types it suits. Metalized for premium shelf presence, aluminium foil for maximum barrier, nylon for liquids, PET for showing the product, kraft for brands positioned as natural.

The press deserves its own moment for a different reason. HP Indigo 20000 is the reason small runs can look like big-brand work, so it is framed as a benefit list rather than a spec sheet: rich colour, sharp detail, luxury finishing, and small minimum orders without plate costs.

flexypack.co.id/#material
A colour per materialMetalized, aluminium, nylon, PET and kraft each carry their own accent, so the material becomes recognisable across the site.
Suitability as chipsSerum, vitamin, lotion, hair care. The buyer matches their product to a material without reading a table.
flexypack.co.id/#teknologi
The press section, written as four promises instead of a specification.

The visual system

Written down as a style profile, so the site survives the next person who touches it

SECTION 03

Colourful-premium, on a budget of one typeface

The brief was a contradiction: premium enough for beauty, friendly enough for a founder ordering a hundred pouches.

The system resolves it with four stated personality traits, and every decision below is traceable to one of them: modern (clean, generous breathing room, rounded corners), colourful-premium (a violet-to-blue gradient with bold pink and yellow accents that stay elegant), friendly (warm language, no jargon), and trustworthy (social proof, statistics, and tidy detail).

Blue#2D50E6Primary button, link
Blue Deep#1F3AB8Hover, gradient
Navy#2E3192Headings
Violet#7A2FF0Gradient end
Pink#F0348BCTA, eyebrow
Yellow#FFC633Secondary CTA
Ink#23264ABody text
BG Soft#F6F8FESection ground

One typeface, five sizes

Montserrat throughout, capped at weight 700 so nothing turns heavy. Hero around 39px, section headings no larger than 22px, card titles 18px, body 15px, captions 11 to 12px. Five steps is enough for a page this long, and the cap keeps a colourful layout from shouting.

Roles, not favouritesPrimary builds structure and trust, accent drives action, neutral carries text and ground. Every swatch is labelled with the job it does.
Materials get their own accentsA separate row of five so a material keeps its identity wherever it appears on the page.
The colour system, as handed over: primary, accent, neutral, material accents, feature-card solids, dark tones and gradients.

Responsive by rule, not by eye

Three breakpoints, one spacing scale, and a table that settles every argument

SECTION 04

The same page, two postures

Every gap on the site comes off a 4px scale with an 8px rhythm, from a 4px icon gap up to 76px of vertical section padding on desktop. Content is capped at 1216px, and the gutter steps down with the viewport: 32px above 961px, 24px between 601 and 960, 16px at 600 and below.

That means the mobile layout is not a squeeze of the desktop one. Sections lose 22px of vertical padding, large call-to-action banners lose 24px of inner padding, cards lose 6px, while buttons and chips keep exactly the same padding so touch targets never shrink. The rules were written down before the mobile file was drawn.

flexypack.co.id
Six across becomes six downThe numbered steps keep their oversized figures on mobile; only the axis changes, so the rhythm of the block survives.
Touch targets holdButtons and chips carry identical padding at every width. Only the space around them is allowed to shrink.
One block, both postures. The desktop file is 1440 wide, the mobile file 390.
ElementDesktopMobile
Section, top and bottom76px54px
Banner / large CTA, inner56px32px
Standard card28px22px
Card body (material, category)20–22px18px
Primary button13px · 28px13px · 28px
Chip / tag4px · 12px4px · 12px
Announcement bar height44px44px
Navbar height70px64px
Section heading to content44px44px

Taken from the style profile. The last three rows are the interesting ones: the announcement bar, the button padding and the gap under a heading stay fixed, because shrinking them is what makes a mobile page feel cramped rather than compact.

flexypack.co.id
The spacing scale and page margins, beside the gallery as it lands on a phone.
SECTION 05

Earning
the enquiry

By the time someone reaches the form, the page should have answered the questions they were too polite to ask.

The lower half of the page carries the weight of trust: production statistics, brands already printed, a short library of articles for people still learning, video and written testimonials, and a frequently asked questions block that takes the awkward subjects head on. Minimum order, lead time, whether they ship nationwide, what happens if a design is wrong.

Every one of those answers exists because it was a question that used to arrive in chat. Putting them on the page does two jobs at once: it removes friction for the buyer, and it shortens the sales conversation for the team.

flexypack.co.id/#faq
Awkward questions firstMinimum order and production time lead the list, because those are the two that stop a founder from enquiring at all.
One closing askAfter the answers, a single call to action. No competing buttons, no second form.
SECTION 06

Reflection

The site was the visible deliverable. The style profile is the one that keeps working.

A marketing page is rarely finished. Someone will add a section, run a promotion, change a photograph. Handing over a written system, colour roles, a five-step type scale, a spacing table and component anatomy, means those future edits stay inside the design rather than slowly dissolving it.

If I took another pass, I would spend it on the middle of the page. The gallery and the article library both ask for attention at the same moment, and I suspect the articles would work harder further down, after the price question has already been raised.

Write the rules down, and the twentieth section still looks like the first.
